title: The shortest great sutra
hook: a few lines on the perfection of wisdom, chanted daily across East Asia and Tibet; read in Müller's 1894 translation

segments.voice: Yesterday: your four foundations. Your line was four places to stand: body, feelings, mind, dhammas. Did you find the body first when you felt lost? Day two hundred sixty-seven, and a new part of the path.
screen: `YOUR FOUR FOUNDATIONS — FOUR PLACES TO STAND.`

segments.voice: A whole teaching on wisdom, on a single page. That's what the next part of the path holds. It's short enough to chant before a kettle boils, yet in that space it tries to say what wisdom sees, and it ends with a few syllables meant to be said out loud. Monks chant it from memory; so do lay people at home altars. For the next ten days, we'll read it slowly, line by line. Today's word: prajnaparamita, the perfection of wisdom.
screen: `A WHOLE TEACHING ON ONE PAGE.` → `CHANTED FROM MEMORY.` → `TEN DAYS, LINE BY LINE.`

segments.voice: Its full name is the Heart of the Perfection of Wisdom Sutra, usually just called the Heart Sutra. It belongs to the Mahayana, the branch of Buddhism found across East Asia, Tibet, Mongolia and Vietnam. Theravada Buddhists, who have walked with us through the Pali texts these past weeks, don't use it as scripture; it comes from a different family of texts, and both families are honored by their own communities. Prajnaparamita is two Sanskrit words. Prajna is wisdom, the deep seeing that understands how things really are. Paramita is perfection, but there's a famous traditional reading of it: para, the far shore, and ita, gone. Wisdom gone beyond. Wisdom that has crossed over. Some modern scholars trace the word instead to parama, the highest. But the image of crossing has stuck, and the text itself will use it. There's a whole library of perfection-of-wisdom texts, some of them enormous; one is even named for its hundred thousand lines. The Heart Sutra is their heart: the whole teaching pressed into a page. There's also an English connection. In the eighteen eighties, Max Müller in Oxford, working with the Japanese scholar Bunyiu Nanjio, published the Sanskrit text from old palm leaves kept at the temple of Horyuji in Japan. Müller's English translation appeared in eighteen ninety-four. So it's a short text, with a very long reach.
screen: `THE HEART OF THE PERFECTION OF WISDOM.` · `A MAHAYANA TEXT.` · `PRAJNA + PARAMITA: WISDOM GONE BEYOND.` · `PALM LEAVES AT HORYUJI.` · then, large: `WISDOM GONE BEYOND.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. For now, let the sit be simple: rest with the breath, and hold one phrase lightly, wisdom gone beyond. Picture a river, and the far shore. Don't try to cross. Just know the shore is there. Later today, if you'd like, find a copy of the Heart Sutra, Müller's translation is freely available, and read it once, slowly, out loud if you can. Don't try to understand it yet. The bell holds the time.
Prajnaparamita. The perfection of wisdom, or, in the old reading, wisdom gone beyond: the heart of a whole library, pressed into one page.
Your line: wisdom gone beyond. Today, read the Heart Sutra once, slowly, in any translation you have, and notice one line that catches you. Day two hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: The Heart Sutra is chanted daily in many Zen, Chan, Korean Seon and Tibetan communities, often at morning and evening services; Theravada communities do not use it as scripture.

fork.setup: you're a Buddhist in Sri Lanka and a friend from Japan asks if you chant the Heart Sutra every morning. what's the likeliest answer?

original.note: Sanskrit prajñāpāramitā: the perfection of wisdom.

trapdoor: what you thought: prajnaparamita is a name, maybe a goddess.
what it means: the perfection of wisdom, read traditionally as wisdom gone beyond.

what a scholar hears: the pāram + itā ('gone to the far shore') reading is traditional; modern philologists prefer pāramī (from parama, highest) + tā; and prajñāpāramitā is also personified as a goddess in later Indian and Tibetan art.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: new hook (the old one opened 'Walk into a Zen temple in Kyoto', the same tour of temples as days 275 and 276, and gave an uncited ~260-character count); myth item on the character count replaced; 'scholars today think' softened to 'some modern scholars'; 'for centuries' dropped; the hundred-thousand-line text named by its title.

Müller's 1894 translation (SBE 49) is referred to but not quoted: it is not on the validator's list of public-domain translations and its wording was not verified. If added to the list, later Heart Sutra days could quote it.
Müller and Nanjio published the Horyuji palm-leaf text in Anecdota Oxoniensia (1884); confirm date and details. The Horyuji manuscript's traditional date (early 7th c.) is disputed by scholars.
Character count (~260) refers to Xuanzang's Chinese version; confirm.
Etymology of pāramitā: traditional vs. philological readings are both presented.
Theravada/Mahayana difference stated without ranking; please check tone.
